transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Alvarez (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Redwood Solutions), Jenna Park (Silverlake Security Lead), Omar Rahman (Silverlake DevOps), Priya Patel (Silverlake Eng Mgr), Liam O'Neill (Compliance)

Summary: Weekly POC security sync focused on SSO (Okta/SAML), audit logs export and retention, encryption/KMS, SOC2 evidence, and next steps for pilot tuning. Discussed dataset handling during pilot, redaction, and SIEM integration.

00:00 - Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick agenda - SSO, audit logs, retention, SOC2 questions, then next steps.
00:14 - Jenna: great, yea, thanks. we had a few questions after last week's notes, mostly around retention and whether logs can be pushed to our splunk, and also we want to make sure okta configuration won't require any firewall changes.
00:32 - Carlos: cool, quick note - we support SAML2.0 via Okta; most customers use inbound SAML for console SSO and SCIM for provisioning. for the private deployment we can do SAML over the customer VPN as well.
00:48 - Omar: when you say private deployment, do you mean VPC peering or on-prem package? cause we have strict egress controls, so peering might be easier but we need clarification on ports and hostnames.
01:05 - Maya: right, and to clarify, for the pilot you're on dedicated reserved pool in our private tenant, we can also run the on-prem bundle if needed. Carlos, can you speak to networking?
01:18 - Carlos: sure - for VPC mode we require outbound to our control plane on 443 to a small set of IPs, or alternately the on-prem agent can run with zero egress if you want fully air-gapped. Firewall rules are doc'd in the tech spec.
01:35 - Priya: okay that's good, air-gapped might be overkill for the pilot, but we need the list of IPs and cert fingerprints for the peering setup.
01:49 - Carlos: noted, will include that.
02:03 - Jenna: on audit logs - can you confirm what events are captured? we need a per-request audit trail tied to user identity, model version, prompt hashes, and token counts.
02:19 - Carlos: yes, we emit request-level logs including user id, route/model, timestamp, latency and token usage. we also include a request id so you can tie traces to your SIEM. there may be redaction options for prompt content - by default the pilot keeps plain prompts but we can enable prompt-redaction to hash or drop inputs.
02:41 - Liam: hashing is ok for PII but we need to be able to run forensics if there's a compliance incident. how reversible are those hashes?
02:55 - Carlos: hashes are one-way; the recommended approach is to store a hashed key in your SIEM and keep full plaintexts in a secure vault with strict RBAC if you need reversibility. for banking customers we typically recommend retaining plaintext for 90 days and hashed indexes longer term.
03:18 - Omar: retention - regulator wants 7 years for some records; are you able to support long-term archival of logs?
03:30 - Samir: yes, audit logs can be exported to S3 (or your object store) with lifecycle policies; we can set retention to meet regulatory requirements and provide immutable storage via object lock if you want.
03:48 - Jenna: will exported logs contain prompts? we need to ensure PII is handled before pushing to our long-term store.
03:58 - Carlos: export is flexible - you can choose to export full logs, or use a transformation step that redacts sensitive fields. we can provide the lambda/transform example to run prior to storage.
04:18 - Priya: about SOC2 - you shared the compliance pack last week, we had a couple follow-ups: encryption key handling (KMS vs HSM), key rotation, and auditability of key access.
04:32 - Maya: quick answer - we use KMS for hosted and Dedicated, HSM integrations for Private when customers require hardware-backed keys. key rotation is supported; access to keys is logged and part of our audit trail.
04:47 - Liam: does your SOC2 cover the private deployment when run in our environment?
04:55 - Maya: our SOC2 report covers Redwood's control plane and hosted/dedicated managed environments. for fully on-prem deployments under customer control, the SOC2 doesn't extend to your data center controls - we provide guidance and runbooks to help. we can also provide a shared responsibilities doc.
05:15 - Jenna: can you share redwood's SOC2 scope and any bridge letters?
05:24 - Maya: yes, i'll send the SOC2 summary, the full audit excerpt is under NDA but we can provide the summary and control mapping.
05:33 - Carlos: also sending network diagram and the minimal ports table.
05:40 - Omar: SIEM integration - we are running Splunk on-prem, want to ingest logs in near real-time. what's the easiest pattern?
05:52 - Carlos: stream logs via HTTPS to your collector endpoint, or push to S3 and have Splunk ingest from S3. for near real-time we recommend direct HTTPS push with auth via mTLS or token - we'll provide the sample config.
06:10 - Jenna: ok, any limitations on log throughput? the pilot sees ~500 rps during peak tests.
06:22 - Carlos: our log pipeline is designed for high throughput; we might recommend batching for cost reasons, but throughput is supported. we'll validate during benchmark tests.
06:36 - Priya: about SSO provisioning - we want SCIM to manage service accounts for the pilot, zap creation and deprovisioning. supported?
06:46 - Maya: yes, SCIM is supported for user provisioning, group sync, deprovisioning. we map roles to RBAC in the console.
06:56 - Omar: role mapping - can we enforce least privilege so only certain roles can request high-cost models?
07:06 - Carlos: yes, RBAC policies can be scoped by model and by route. we have policy objects that let you define who can call which model/profile.
07:18 - Jenna: data residency - some datasets we use for testing are EU-only, can we pin the model region?
07:28 - Maya: you can pin region at workspace or route level. for the pilot we can ensure EU region hosting for those requests.
07:39 - Priya: question re: telemetry - does Redwood collect usage telemetry beyond logs (metrics, traces) for optimizing batching? and is that PII-free?
07:52 - Carlos: we collect anonymized metrics for runtime optimization by default; we can disable telemetry for your pilot if you prefer. any identifiable material is considered customer data and subject to the contract.
08:10 - Liam: do you provide penetration test results for the service?
08:18 - Maya: yes, we can share pentest summaries and remediation items; full reports require an NDA.
08:27 - Jenna: good. also, can you describe how you would handle an incident where a prompt included PII and got logged - what's your incident response?
08:40 - Carlos: incident response: notify customer within SLA window, provide a forensics package (request ids, timestamps, raw logs if available), and work with the customer to remediate. if prompt contains PII we can run an on-demand purge for the pilot data store and verify deletion.
09:02 - Priya: purge - is deletion from caches immediate? for the KV cache / chat contexts?
09:12 - Carlos: we can invalidate KV cache entries tied to a request id; for longer-running retained contexts there may be a short window where data persists in memory across replicas, but we have controls to scrub and rotate caches. we'll detail this in the runbook.
09:35 - Maya: ok moving to tuning - last week's quality tests showed token usage variance; we recommended small prompt templating changes and enabling prefix caching for common prompts. any blockers to enabling caching?
09:49 - Priya: none, but we need to ensure caching doesn't leak cross-tenant data, which is a hard requirement.
09:59 - Carlos: isolation is enforced - caches are namespaced by tenant and model-version. we also keep a strict tenant-id check on retrieval.
10:12 - Omar: one more on encryption - for the pilot will Redwood manage keys or do we want customer-managed keys? pros/cons?
10:24 - Samir: managed KMS is easiest; customer-managed gives you more control and reduces scope for us but increases your key ops. for production banks often prefer CMEK (customer-managed encryption keys) via HSM.
10:40 - Jenna: we need proof-of-concept with CMEK for the final phase, can that be scheduled?
10:47 - Maya: yes, we'll scope CMEK in the next phase, Carlos will estimate effort.
10:54 - Carlos: rough estimate: 2-3 days of engineering to swap key provider in Dedicated/Private mode and test rotation flows.
11:05 - Priya: testing timeline - we plan to run a compliance benchmark week of 2026-08-10. can Redwood be ready to provide logs and keys testing then?
11:17 - Maya: yes, target to have export and SCIM/SSO validated by then; we'll prioritize network details this week.
11:28 - Omar: any problems with our egress rules if we do direct HTTPS log push? we block outbound to unknown hosts currently.
11:38 - Carlos: you can either open a specific IP range and FQDNs, or use an agent to forward logs from inside your network to Redwood. we'll provide both patterns.
11:51 - Jenna: one final question - retention costs: is long-term archive billed differently?
11:59 - Maya: yes, archive storage (S3 glacier-like) is cheaper and billed separately; we'll include cost estimates for 3/7 year retention in the pricing deck.
12:12 - Maya (recap): ok to recap next steps - Redwood to send SOC2 summary, network IPs, and sample log export + transform. Customer to provide Okta test account and retention requirements. agree?
12:26 - Jenna: yes, that works.
12:32 - Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and update the pilot plan doc.

References shared: Redwood SOC2 summary (link: https://redwood.example/sec/soc2-summary.pdf), Network ports table (link: https://redwood.example/net/ports.csv), Sample log transform lambda (link: https://github.com/redwood/example-log-transform).

Notes about transcription: occasional speaker misattribution and some words transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cache" as "kay vee cache"), filler words present.

End of meeting.
